INSERT INTO course_lessons (moduleId, slug, title, orderIndex, content, linkedScenarioId, estimatedMinutes, isPublished) VALUES (30005, 'intermittent-fault-diagnosis', 'Intermittent Fault Diagnosis: Finding the Ghost in the Machine', 7, '## The Hardest Faults to Find

Intermittent faults are the bane of every maintenance technician''s existence. The machine faults once a shift, or once a day, or only when it''s hot, or only on Tuesdays. By the time you arrive, everything looks normal. You can''t reproduce it. You can''t measure it. You can''t find it.

But it''s there. And it will come back.

This lesson teaches you the strategies and techniques for finding intermittent faults—the ones that make experienced technicians pull their hair out.

## Why Intermittent Faults Are Different

A solid fault (motor burned out, wire cut, fuse blown) is easy to find because the evidence is always present. You measure, you find it, you fix it.

An intermittent fault only manifests under specific conditions:

| Trigger | Example | Why It''s Hard |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Thermal | Loose connection that opens when hot | Works fine when you test it cold |
| Vibration | Cracked solder joint on a circuit board | Works fine when machine is stopped |
| Load | Contactor that chatters under high current | Works fine at low load |
| Time | Capacitor that drifts out of spec after warmup | Works fine for the first 2 hours |
| Position | Cable that opens at a specific robot position | Works fine in home position |
| Moisture | Insulation breakdown when humidity is high | Works fine on dry days |

## Strategy 1: Data Collection Over Time

Since you can''t catch the fault in the act, collect data that captures it:

### PLC Fault Logs

Every PLC records fault events with timestamps. Pull the fault history and look for patterns:
- Same time every day? (Temperature-related—afternoon heat)
- Same point in the machine cycle? (Position or load-related)
- Correlates with a specific product? (Recipe or weight-related)
- Correlates with a specific operator? (Operational procedure issue)

### Trend Data

SCADA and HMI systems record process variables over time. Look for:
- Gradual drift before the fault (sensor degradation)
- Sudden spikes (electrical noise or momentary shorts)
- Oscillation (control loop instability)

### Event Correlation

Cross-reference the fault timestamps with other plant events:
- Does it happen when the large press on the same feeder starts? (Voltage sag)
- Does it happen during shift change? (Different operating procedures)
- Does it happen after maintenance on adjacent equipment? (Something was disturbed)

## Strategy 2: Environmental Manipulation

If you suspect a thermal or vibration-related fault, create the conditions:

### Thermal Testing

- **Heat gun method:** Carefully apply heat to suspected components (connections, relays, circuit boards) while monitoring for the fault. If heating a specific terminal causes the fault, you''ve found your loose connection.
- **Freeze spray method:** Cool suspected components with freeze spray. If cooling a component makes the fault go away (or appear), that component is thermally sensitive.

> **CAUTION:** Use heat guns carefully around wiring—don''t melt insulation. And never use freeze spray on energized high-voltage components.

### Vibration Testing

- **Tap test:** While the machine is running, gently tap on suspected components (terminal blocks, connectors, circuit boards) with an insulated tool. If tapping causes the fault, you''ve found a loose connection or cracked joint.
- **Wiggle test:** Gently flex cables and connectors while monitoring for signal dropout.

## Strategy 3: Substitution and Isolation

### The Swap Test

If you have two identical channels (e.g., two identical sensors on two identical stations), swap them:
- If the problem follows the component: the component is faulty
- If the problem stays in the same location: the wiring or environment is the issue

### The Isolation Test

Disconnect suspected interference sources one at a time:
- Disconnect the VFD output and run the motor across-the-line. Does the fault go away? (VFD-generated noise)
- Move the signal cable away from power cables. Does the fault go away? (EMI coupling)
- Add a filter or shielding to a specific signal. Does the fault go away? (Noise susceptibility)

## Strategy 4: Continuous Monitoring

When all else fails, set up monitoring and wait:

### Min/Max Recording

Many digital multimeters have a MIN/MAX recording mode. Connect to the suspected circuit and leave it recording. When the fault occurs, the MIN or MAX reading will capture the anomaly.

### Data Loggers

For long-term monitoring, use a data logger connected to the suspected signal. Record for days or weeks if necessary. The data will eventually capture the event.

## Common Intermittent Fault Patterns

### The Thermal Connection

**Pattern:** Fault occurs after 2-3 hours of operation, clears after cooldown.
**Cause:** A loose terminal connection that has high resistance. As current flows, the connection heats up (I-squared-R heating). As it heats, it expands and the resistance increases further (positive feedback loop). Eventually it opens completely or causes enough voltage drop to trip a fault.
**Fix:** Re-torque all connections in the circuit. Look for discolored terminals (heat damage).

### The Vibration Crack

**Pattern:** Fault occurs during specific machine operations that create vibration.
**Cause:** A cracked solder joint on a circuit board, or a broken wire strand inside insulation that only separates under vibration.
**Fix:** Inspect circuit boards under magnification. Flex cables while monitoring continuity.

### The EMI Ghost

**Pattern:** Fault occurs when a nearby VFD or large motor starts, or when welding is happening in the area.
**Cause:** Electromagnetic interference coupling into signal wiring.
**Fix:** Proper cable routing (separate power and signal), shielding, filtering, or fiber optic conversion for critical signals.

### The Moisture Fault

**Pattern:** Fault occurs on humid days, rainy days, or Monday mornings (after weekend shutdown allows condensation).
**Cause:** Moisture on insulation surfaces creating leakage paths, or inside connectors causing corrosion.
**Fix:** Seal enclosures, add heaters to panels in humid environments, replace corroded connectors.

## Documentation Is Critical

For intermittent faults, your documentation IS your diagnostic tool:

- Record every occurrence with date, time, conditions, and what was happening
- Record what you checked and what you found (even if you found nothing)
- Record environmental conditions (temperature, humidity, production rate)
- After 3-5 occurrences, patterns will emerge that point to the root cause

## The Patience Factor

Intermittent faults test your patience and your ego. You might not solve it on the first call, or the second, or the third. That''s normal. The key is to collect data on every occurrence, eliminate possibilities systematically, and resist the urge to replace expensive components "just in case." Systematic data collection will eventually reveal the pattern.', 9, 25, 1);
